name: Generic Viridian
lede: Generic Viridian is a blue-green standing in for the pigment family named viridian, Latin for green, without claiming to be any one maker's exact hue.

sections.title: A stand-in, not a specific paint
sections.body:
Viridian itself is a chromium oxide pigment, prized by painters for a cool, transparent green unlike the older, more yellow chrome greens [1]. "Generic" in the name signals that this swatch is an average stand-in, not a single manufacturer's tube color, the role the library gives it [1]. Our library finds only a Wikipedia list behind the name, with no date for its coining [1].

Measured in LCH, it sits at lightness 47 with a strong blue-leaning green hue [1]. Its nearest named neighbors are near-ties: [[blue-green]] and [[blue-green]], each within 3 units of CIEDE2000 and described as almost the same [1]. [[spanish-viridian]] and [[arsenate]] sit a little farther out, also close [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This exact swatch is rare in our archive: only 12 of 23,781 paintings match it, rarer than 77 percent of the named colors, as photographed [2]. The earliest matching painting is from 1827, by T. Davies, with the latest from 1959, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. Viridian the pigment was only patented in 1838, so a true viridian green could not appear before then; any earlier match here is this swatch's chromium-free cousins, not the pigment itself [1][2]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [2].

questions.q: What does "generic" signal in this color's name?
choices: It is an average stand-in, not one maker's exact pigment
It was the first color ever named
It means the pigment is toxic
questions.answer: It is an average stand-in, not one maker's exact pigment
